title: Caged in a fantasy, teachers are angry at Hattie
author: Stephen Vainker
summary: Stephen Vainker uses news of a University of Melbourne investigation into John Hattie, and the anger of Australian teachers toward him, to critique the Visible Learning project itself. He traces it to Herbert Walbergs schooling-as-agricultural-plant model, in which every possible influence on learning is an input to be measured, and argues that a student is not a plant and the interplay of educational inputs is far more complex. He holds that Hattie inherited and worsened the problems of effect-size comparison by ranking influences in a league table and mixing comparative with absolute measures, and he alleges plagiarism and incorrect effect sizes. The practical cost, he argues, is that administrators armed with a spurious comprehensive model impose trivial or improbable routines while ignoring class size, teacher expertise, and behaviour. He closes by cautioning that overconfident prescriptions, including Ofsteds, leave teachers caged in a fantasy.
points: The agricultural input-output model behind Visible Learning is a useful lens but a distorting blueprint, because student learning cannot be measured and optimized like crop yield.
Effect-size league tables are unreliable bases for comparing influences, and the author claims Hattie compounded the flaw by mixing measures and mis-extracting effect sizes.
Administrators who adopt a comprehensive research model become overconfident and impose routines like copying learning objectives while ignoring class size and behaviour.
Saying some practices reliably work is different from claiming to know the optimal combination of every influence.
Ofsteds expectation that disadvantaged pupils should catch up is offered as another case of overconfident, structure-blind prescription.
quotes: Amongst the various ideas for transforming schools into more business-like organisations, Herbert Walberg proposed a model based on schooling-as-agricultural-plant, where learning is the ‘output’ and every single possible influence on increasing learning is the ‘input’.
This is not to say that schooling is far too unpredictable and complex to manage. It is true that there are certain practices and approaches that can reliably lead to student learning.

The danger, however, is that in trying to be so specific in such a complex environment, that administrators are not only working from a distorted picture, but that they become overconfident in the scope of their influence. Out of the research, it could be that some factors are thrown up as being far more important than they really are, while others are downplayed.

From Walberg, he inherited the problem of presenting ‘effect size’ as though it provided the basis for a reliable comparison between influences (it does no such thing). However, he exarcebated the problem by producing a league table of specific influences.

Education needs prescriptions - confident expectations of what schools and teachers should do. But we live in an era of overconfident and often misleading prescriptions that mean teachers are caged in a fantasy as they deal with the hugely demanding realities of day-to-day schooling.

As I explain in this piece, his approach to ‘scientifically’ modelling the entirety of schooling was always hubristic. Like an Adam Curtis doc, it is a story of someone who promised to provide a comprehensive, rationalised approach to schooling, who instead created a fantasy that others were forced to live in.
